topic: gender bias in MT / BLEU evaluation
hypothesis_a: Lower gender bias correlates with better translation quality as measured by BLEU score; prior work reports BLEU gains from gender-control methods (escude-font-costa-jussa-2019-equalizing, stanovsky-etal-2019-evaluating, basta-jussa-2020-mitigating).
hypothesis_b: Previously obtained BLEU gains cannot be ascribed with certainty to a better control of gender features in machine translation.
rationale_A: Same observed evidence (BLEU gains); B disputes the causal attribution to gender control specifically, not the gain itself
rationale_B: B disputes whether BLEU gains can be credibly attributed to gender control; a methodological critique of the causal attribution, not an independent counter-claim.

topic: indirect gender bias in word embeddings
hypothesis_a: Indirect bias in word embeddings (via projection onto a gender subspace, e.g. 'businessman'/'genius' closer to 'football') is a real, detectable phenomenon; existing projection-based debiasing methods (e.g. Bolukbasi et al. 2016) address gender bias in embeddings.
hypothesis_b: Indirect bias has been disregarded to some extent by existing methods, and mitigation methods for indirect bias are not provided by the current debiasing approaches.
rationale_A: Surface tension over whether current debiasing methods address indirect bias; resolves once scope of 'method' claims is clarified -- borderline with type1
rationale_B: A says existing debiasing methods address gender bias in embeddings; B directly negates this for indirect bias specifically, calling it disregarded/unaddressed.

topic: causal source of MT context-based debiasing gains
hypothesis_a: Concatenating the previous sentence as additional context (only in the decoder) improves machine translation performance on coreference-resolution tasks, attributed to added gender context.
hypothesis_b: This improvement is not necessarily due to the added gender context, but may instead be a regularisation effect from the additional training signal.
rationale_A: Same observed MT improvement, literally opposite proposed cause: gender context vs regularisation artifact -- textbook causal conflict
rationale_B: Same observed effect (context-concatenation improves coref/translation) attributed to two incompatible causes: added gender context vs. mere regularization from extra signal.

hypothesis_a: Adversarial learning can remove model bias by explicitly protecting demographic information (such as gender) during model training, producing representations without the protected attribute.
hypothesis_b: Word representations trained with adversarial removal still preserve traces of the protected attributes; external verification of the method is needed because the removal is not actually complete.
rationale_A: A: bias is explicitly removed/protected during training. B: representations still preserve traces of the same protected attribute. Direct negation under the same method class
rationale_B: A claims adversarial training removes the protected attribute entirely; B directly negates this, showing traces of the attribute persist despite training.

topic: completeness of fine-tuning-based gender debiasing for MT
hypothesis_a: Training on a larger corpus then fine-tuning with a gender-balanced corpus successfully mitigates gender bias and increases translation performance quality, even across domains.
hypothesis_b: This fine-tuning approach does not account for the qualitative differences in how men and women are portrayed in the resulting translations -- surface bias metrics improve but portrayal-level bias remains unaddressed.
rationale_A: A claims success on measured bias/quality metrics; B says a different, unmeasured dimension (portrayal nuance) is unaddressed -- compatible once scope is separated, but real surface tension
rationale_B: Differ by measurement scope: A claims success on surface bias/quality metrics; B shows portrayal-level bias persists. Compatible once scope is distinguished.

hypothesis_a: Studies of gender in movie dialogue consistently show female characters are portrayed with more positive language, fewer references to death, and fewer swear words compared to male characters.
hypothesis_b: High-agency women frames (women portrayed as active agents driving the plot) are rare in modern films, despite the more positive language found in prior portrayal studies.
rationale_A: Different measured constructs (sentiment/positivity of language vs narrative agency) -- a character can be positively described yet low-agency; not incompatible
rationale_B: Different constructs measured (language positivity vs. narrative agency); apparent tension dissolves once distinguished -- positive language doesn't imply high agency.

topic: trend of gender bias in text over time / historical persistence
hypothesis_a: Unsupervised analysis of literature finds differences between descriptions of males and females align with common, persistent gender stereotypes (e.g. positive adjectives for women more often relate to their bodies).
hypothesis_b: Gender bias in text has in fact decreased over the last 100 years, with the women's movement of the 1960s-70s having a significant, measurable effect on women's portrayals in literature and culture.
rationale_A: Persistent-stereotype snapshot vs declining-bias-over-100-years trend use different methods/timeframes (static analysis vs longitudinal historical embeddings); could be compatible (bias declining but retaining stereotype direction)
rationale_B: Different scope: A reports persistent stereotype patterns (cross-sectional); B reports a decreasing bias trend (longitudinal). Not directly opposed once scope is separated.

hypothesis_a: Powerful women are frequently portrayed in the media, though typically described as less powerful than their actual societal role.
hypothesis_b: There is, in fact, a measurable gender gap in the overall coverage of women in Canadian news outlets.
rationale_A: 'Frequently portrayed but less powerful framing' and 'coverage gap relative to men' are not mutually exclusive -- genuinely compatible, not a real dispute
rationale_B: Different scope/dataset: A concerns power-framing within powerful-women coverage; B concerns overall coverage-volume gender gap. Distinct measures, apparently compatible.

topic: validity of PMI as a gender-bias measure
hypothesis_a: Words with high pointwise mutual information (PMI) values for one gender are suggested to have high gender bias, and PMI is used as a bias-detection metric.
hypothesis_b: Bias measured at the level of word co-occurrences (PMI) is likely to lead to overgeneralisation when applied to a heterogeneous dataset, undermining PMI as a reliable bias metric.
rationale_A: Critique of a widely-used metric (PMI) rather than two specific competing hypotheses; paradigm-level methodological tension, similar to round-1 p009/p021 pattern
rationale_B: B is a methodological critique of PMI's reliability as a bias metric (overgeneralization on heterogeneous data), not an independent competing empirical claim.

topic: label-preservation assumption in adversarial text perturbation
hypothesis_a: Small text perturbations used for adversarial robustness evaluation (token/character swapping, paraphrasing, semantically-equivalent rules, distractor insertion) preserve the gold label of the original example -- a foundational assumption underlying this line of NLP robustness research.
hypothesis_b: A significant portion of perturbed examples produced by these existing text perturbation techniques are NOT actually label-preserving, and the resulting labels often show high disagreement among human raters -- the perturbations can even fool humans, not just models.
rationale_A: A: perturbations preserve the gold label (assumption). B: a significant portion do NOT preserve the label for the same technique class -- direct empirical negation of a stated assumption under the same conditions
rationale_B: A asserts perturbations preserve gold labels (foundational assumption); B directly found a significant portion do not, with high human disagreement, same techniques/conditions.

hypothesis_a: Locate-then-edit knowledge-editing methods (ROME, MEMIT) effectively locate and update the relevant model parameters to edit factual knowledge, with MEMIT enabling simultaneous integration of thousands of edits across multiple layers.
hypothesis_b: These methods (ROME, MEMIT) lack non-trivial generalization capabilities, with varying performance and applicability across different model architectures -- the best-performing methods empirically only work well on decoder-only LLMs.
rationale_A: B doesn't say the methods fail entirely, but that their claimed effectiveness doesn't generalize beyond decoder-only architectures -- a scope/condition qualification, not a flat negation
rationale_B: B qualifies scope rather than flatly negating A: methods still work but generalize less broadly than implied, varying by model architecture.

topic: validity of NLI-trained classifiers for faithfulness/inconsistency detection
hypothesis_a: NLI-trained classifiers (trained on natural language inference datasets) are an effective, principled approach for detecting factual inaccuracies and faithfulness errors in generated summaries, based on the idea that faithful content should be entailed by its source.
hypothesis_b: There is a mismatch in input granularity between conventional NLI datasets and inconsistency-detection datasets, which limits the applicability of NLI-trained classifiers for effectively detecting inconsistencies in generated text.
rationale_A: B is a methodological critique of NLI-classifiers' applicability for a specific subtask (granularity mismatch), not an independent competing claim -- same pattern as round-3 PMI/BLEU critiques
rationale_B: B is a methodological critique of an assumption NLI classifiers rely on (input-granularity mismatch), limiting applicability rather than negating effectiveness outright.

topic: whether modifying attention heads changes model output
hypothesis_a: Modifying the encoder-decoder attention heads DOES substantially influence machine translation model generations -- attention weights are causally meaningful to the model's output.
hypothesis_b: In single-sequence (non-encoder-decoder) tasks, modifying/perturbing attention weights does NOT substantially change model predictions -- attention is not causally necessary for the output in that setting.
rationale_A: Explicit 'in contrast to' framing by survey author; A and B are attributed to different task setups (encoder-decoder MT vs single-sequence classification) -- resolves once task type is accounted for, matches the real attention-as-explanation debate
rationale_B: Both hypotheses explicitly scope to different task setups (encoder-decoder MT vs. single-sequence classification); findings are condition-dependent, not a same-condition negation.

topic: practical viability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) vs MLPs
hypothesis_a: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) offer a high degree of functional transparency via learnable univariate spline functions on edges, making them 'symbolic-friendly' -- trained KANs can be pruned and simplified into concise mathematical expressions.
hypothesis_b: KANs often suffer from significant computational overhead, optimization instability, and inferior performance compared to standard MLPs, especially as model size or input dimensionality grows -- undermining their practical viability despite the interpretability claims.
rationale_A: A (interpretability/transparency) and B (computational cost/performance vs MLPs) address different dimensions that aren't strictly mutually exclusive, but the survey's 'However' framing signals a real practical complication of KAN's touted benefits
rationale_B: Claims address different dimensions (interpretability/pruning vs. compute cost and performance); B explicitly grants A's interpretability claim while disputing its practical payoff.

topic: optimal number of languages for cross-lingual transfer in multilingual tuning
hypothesis_a: Including just a FEW languages (e.g. 2-4) in multilingual instruction tuning can enhance cross-lingual transfer, especially for languages not encountered during pre-training -- suggesting a small number of languages is optimal.
hypothesis_b: Increasing the NUMBER of languages may further enhance multilingual performance -- suggesting more languages is better, though the optimal number also depends on language similarity and downstream evaluation.
rationale_A: Both about the causal effect of 'number of languages' on multilingual performance/transfer, opposite direction claimed (few is optimal vs more helps) -- explicit 'However' framing by survey author treats them as the same question
rationale_B: Same variable (number of languages) and outcome (cross-lingual transfer), opposite direction claims: fewer languages optimal vs more languages better.

hypothesis_a: Sparse attention (attending to fewer tokens, to reduce computational cost) was explored with the idea/hypothesis that attending to fewer tokens could also improve interpretability.
hypothesis_b: Sparseness does NOT guarantee better interpretability -- adding sparsity decreases plausibility and sparse attention correlates less with other feature-importance measures compared to standard attention, based on controlled experiments on IMDB/SST/20News.
rationale_A: A is a hypothesis that sparsity CAUSES better interpretability; B directly refutes that causal claim with controlled experiments showing sparsity DECREASES plausibility -- same effect, opposite causal direction
rationale_B: Same causal relationship (sparsity of attention vs interpretability) with opposite conclusions: hypothesized to improve it, evidence shows it does not.

hypothesis_a: Attention is not explainable -- attention weights do not provide a faithful/reliable explanation of model predictions.
hypothesis_b: Attention maybe/can be explainable -- disputing the blanket claim that attention weights are never a valid explanation of model predictions.
rationale_A: Clean direct negation: 'attention is not explainable' (A) vs 'attention maybe explainable' (B) -- same general question, two well-known directly-opposing papers in the literature
rationale_B: Flat assertion X (attention not explainable) vs flat assertion not-X (attention can be explainable) about the same general claim, same construct.

topic: Effect of expert evaluators on human evaluation
hypothesis_a: Consulting expert evaluators has a measurable effect on human evaluation outcomes in machine translation: expert-based reassessment showed that neural machine translation had not actually attained human parity, contradicting earlier parity claims based on non-expert evaluation.
hypothesis_b: Consulting expert evaluators does not have a measurable effect on human evaluation outcomes in computational poetry generation: an experiment assessing novelty, meaning, reaction, and craft found no significant benefit from expert involvement (a negative result).
rationale_A: The two claims about whether expert evaluators matter concern different task domains (machine translation vs. computational poetry generation), so the apparent conflict is explained by differing evaluation contexts rather than a real disagreement about the same entities/conditions -- not type1, since "expert evaluators help" and "expert evaluators don't help" are not asserted of the same task.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses apply to different domains (machine translation versus computational poetry generation), so the finding that experts matter in one task but not another is not a contradiction.

hypothesis_a: Manipulating attention weights in encoder-decoder architectures (e.g., neural machine translation) substantially changes model generations, indicating that attention distributions carry information relevant to model behavior in such tasks.
hypothesis_b: In single-sequence tasks, attention weights do not constitute a faithful explanation of a model's predictions: altering the attention distribution often does not meaningfully change model output, so attention is not explanation.
rationale_A: Hypothesis A's claim is scoped to encoder-decoder/seq2seq architectures (e.g., NMT), while hypothesis B's claim is scoped to single-sequence tasks; the difference in conclusion tracks a difference in task/architecture type rather than a genuine same-condition contradiction, distinguishing it from type1/type3 despite the superficially opposite-sounding conclusions.
rationale_B: The hypotheses apply to different task settings—encoder-decoder architectures versus single-sequence tasks—meaning the observed differences in attention sensitivity are context-dependent and not mutually exclusive.

hypothesis_a: Attention weights do not provide a faithful explanation for a model's predictions: adversarial manipulations of attention distributions (e.g., random permutation of weights) often fail to change model outputs, undermining the assumption that attention scores are interpretable ('Attention is not Explanation').
hypothesis_b: Contrary to the claim that attention is not explanation, attention distributions can still serve as plausible explanations of model behavior once methodological issues are addressed, such as accounting for the natural variance attention weights exhibit across training runs ('Attention is not not Explanation').
rationale_A: Hypothesis B is framed as an explicit rebuttal ("Contrary to the claim that attention is not explanation") targeting the same claim about the same object (attention weights as faithful explanations) without restricting itself to a different dataset/architecture/task, so A's negation and B's counter-affirmation are a direct X vs. not-X clash rather than a context-driven (type4) difference.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that attention weights are not a faithful explanation, while Hypothesis B directly negates this by asserting that they can serve as plausible explanations when methodological issues are addressed.

topic: pretraining data frequency and in-context learning
hypothesis_a: In-context learning (few-shot) performance is positively related to how frequently the relevant terms or facts occur in the pretraining data; higher pretraining term frequency is associated with better ICL performance.
hypothesis_b: Pretraining examples containing long-tail, rarely-occurring tokens contribute more significantly to a model's in-context learning ability than frequent, commonly-occurring examples.
rationale_A: Both hypotheses concern the same variables -- pretraining token/example frequency and in-context-learning capability -- but assert opposite directions of the relationship: A says higher term frequency drives better ICL performance, while B says low-frequency (long-tail) examples contribute more to ICL ability than frequent ones; this is a conflict in causal direction, not a quantitative-magnitude dispute (type2) or a dataset/setup artifact (type4), since no differing evaluation conditions are stated in the text.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts a positive relationship between pretraining term frequency and ICL performance, whereas Hypothesis B asserts the opposite, stating that low-frequency (long-tail) tokens contribute more significantly.

hypothesis_a: The success of a computer-generated joke/riddle system for children should be assessed intrinsically, by asking whether the generated items are actually perceived by children as genuine jokes (jokehood), as done for computer-generated punning riddles.
hypothesis_b: The success of a joke-generating system for children (STANDUP) should instead be assessed extrinsically/functionally, by asking whether using the system actually helps users (children with cerebral palsy) improve their real-world social interactions with peers.
rationale_A: A and B propose different evaluation criteria (intrinsic jokehood-perception vs. extrinsic functional/social-outcome assessment), but they apply to different systems and contexts: A concerns a general punning-riddle generator judged on entertainment value, while B concerns STANDUP, an assistive communication device for children with cerebral palsy where the goal is social-skill improvement, not humor perception per se. The apparent clash in 'how success should be assessed' stems from differing system purposes/populations rather than a genuine logical or causal conflict, so the claims are compatible once context is accounted for.
rationale_B: The disagreement in evaluation metrics is explained by the difference in context; Hypothesis A addresses general computational humor, whereas Hypothesis B focuses on a specific therapeutic application (STANDUP) where functional social improvement is the primary goal.

hypothesis_a: Concepts used to explain a model's decisions should be manually pre-defined by the user (e.g., as concept activation vectors in TCAV-style testing), rather than discovered automatically from the model itself.
hypothesis_b: Interpretable abstractions can instead be learned automatically by analyzing individual neurons' activation patterns and composing logical concepts from them; doing so reveals that many neurons actually encode shallow lexical heuristics inherited from dataset biases rather than the clean concepts assumed by manual definitions.
rationale_A: A prescribes that concepts must be manually pre-defined by users rather than discovered automatically; B asserts the opposite, that concepts can instead be learned automatically from neuron activations. Same question (how should interpretability concepts be derived) with directly opposed answers, not a dataset/architecture-driven difference, so type1 rather than type4.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that concepts should be manually pre-defined rather than automatically discovered, whereas Hypothesis B proposes that concepts can and should be learned automatically.

hypothesis_a: Event causality is a key cognitive faculty underlying narrative sense-making, i.e., narrative understanding is fundamentally grounded in identifying causal relations between events.
hypothesis_b: Narrative constitutes a distinct 'narrative mode' of thought that is separate from the 'Paradigmatic/Logico-Scientific Mode' responsible for causal explanation, so narrative sense-making should not be reduced to a causal-reasoning process.
rationale_A: A claims narrative sense-making is fundamentally grounded in causal-relation identification; B claims narrative is a distinct mode of thought that must not be reduced to the causal/logico-scientific mode. These are direct opposite answers to the same question (is narrative understanding fundamentally causal reasoning?), not a contextual artifact, so type1.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that narrative understanding is fundamentally grounded in identifying causal relations, while Hypothesis B explicitly denies this reduction, claiming narrative is a distinct mode of thought separate from causal explanation.

topic: Narrative causality: text vs cognitive process
hypothesis_a: The proper object of study for narrative causality is the narrative text itself, i.e., causality is a structural property of the narrative discourse/form.
hypothesis_b: The proper object of study for narrative causality is the cognitive process of the reader constructing the narrative, i.e., causality is a property of mental representation/comprehension rather than of the text structure.
rationale_A: A locates narrative causality in the text/discourse structure itself; B locates it in the reader's cognitive/mental representation instead. Both address the same question (what is the proper object of study for narrative causality) with mutually exclusive answers, so type1 rather than type4 (no dataset/method confound, just opposed theoretical claims).
rationale_B: The two hypotheses present mutually exclusive claims regarding the fundamental locus of narrative causality, asserting either that it resides in the structural properties of the text or in the cognitive processes of the reader.

topic: LLM-era code-switching: synthetic generation vs zero-shot transfer
hypothesis_a: Synthetic code-mixed data for language modeling can be effectively generated by using linguistic theory (e.g. equivalence-constraint-based mixing) to synthesize training examples, improving code-mixed/code-switched language models.
hypothesis_b: Multilingual large language models are not yet effective code-switchers: despite broad multilingual pretraining, they fail to robustly handle real (naturalistic) code-switching phenomena in zero-shot settings.
rationale_A: A concerns improving code-mixed LMs via linguistically-informed synthetic training data (an explicit training-time intervention), while B concerns the zero-shot code-switching ability of multilingual LLMs with no such intervention. The apparent conflict (one positive, one negative about handling code-switching) dissolves once the different conditions (trained-with-technique vs. untrained zero-shot) are noted, so type4 rather than type1.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A proposes a method for improving models through synthetic data generation, whereas Hypothesis B describes the current performance limitations of LLMs in zero-shot settings; they are not mutually exclusive.

topic: Neural weight-update rules: Hebbian vs Delta
hypothesis_a: The Hebbian learning rule updates synaptic/memory weights via reinforcement-driven, correlation-based updates: connections between co-activated units are strengthened without reference to an explicit target output or error signal.
hypothesis_b: The Delta learning rule updates memory traces via supervised, error-corrective control: weights are adjusted in proportion to the difference between the actual and desired (target) output.
rationale_A: A and B are simply factual descriptions of two different, well-defined learning rules (Hebbian: correlation-based/unsupervised; Delta: error-corrective/supervised). Neither asserts something the other denies about the same rule or phenomenon, so this is not a contradiction of any type.
rationale_B: The hypotheses describe two different, well-established learning mechanisms; defining one as error-free does not contradict the definition of another as error-corrective.

hypothesis_a: ChatGPT can effectively formulate and refine complex Boolean search queries for systematic review literature searches, successfully following user instructions to produce high-quality queries.
hypothesis_b: LLM-based Boolean query generation for systematic reviews does not reliably reproduce or generalize across studies and settings, contradicting claims that well-chosen seed studies reliably improve guided query formulation.
rationale_A: A asserts ChatGPT can effectively and reliably produce high-quality Boolean queries; B explicitly states LLM-based query generation does not reliably reproduce or generalize, directly contradicting that reliability claim. Both are general claims about the same capability (LLM Boolean query generation quality), not attributable to differing eval setups, so type1.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A claims that ChatGPT can effectively and successfully formulate Boolean queries, while Hypothesis B asserts that LLM-based generation is not reliable or generalizable across different settings.

hypothesis_a: Early theorizing on virtual communities (Rheingold, 'The Virtual Community: Homesteading on the Electronic Frontier') held that computer-mediated communication and online communities would foster mutual understanding among participants.
hypothesis_b: Empirical work on online social media (Mathew et al., 'Spread of hate speech in online social media') finds that hate speech spreads widely through these platforms, contradicting hopes that online discussion would primarily promote mutual understanding.
rationale_A: A holds that computer-mediated communication would foster mutual understanding; B shows hate speech spreads widely, explicitly framed as contradicting that hope. This is a direct clash between an expected outcome and its empirical negation for the same phenomenon (effect of online communities on understanding), so type1 rather than type4.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A describes the content of an early theoretical belief, while Hypothesis B describes contemporary empirical findings that refute that belief; both statements can be true at the same time.

hypothesis_a: Apparent 'emergent abilities' of large language models are largely a measurement artifact: using linear/continuous metrics (e.g., token-edit distance) instead of discontinuous metrics like accuracy reveals smooth, continuous, and predictable improvements in model performance with scale, rather than sudden qualitative jumps.
hypothesis_b: Large language models display genuine emergent abilities: capabilities that are essentially absent in smaller-scale models but appear abruptly and unpredictably once a certain scale threshold is crossed.
rationale_A: A claims apparent emergent abilities are a measurement artifact producing smooth, continuous, predictable scaling curves; B claims LLMs display genuine, abrupt, unpredictable emergent jumps. These are mutually exclusive characterizations of the same phenomenon (nature of capability scaling), a classic type1 negation, not a dataset/metric-context reconciliation since the metric-choice explanation is itself what A's claim is built on.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A claims that emergent abilities are a measurement artifact caused by specific metrics, whereas Hypothesis B asserts that these abilities are genuine, intrinsic properties of large-scale models.

hypothesis_a: LLMs generally perform poorly at pinpointing the location of errors within their own reasoning traces, even though they can correct an error once its location is explicitly given to them.
hypothesis_b: Evaluation on ProcessBench shows that reasoning-focused models such as OpenAI's o1 and QwQ achieve remarkable performance at identifying process errors, even on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
rationale_A: A concerns general-purpose LLMs (pre-reasoning-model era, tyen 2024) failing to localize errors in their own reasoning traces; B concerns specialized reasoning-focused models (o1, QwQ) succeeding on the separate ProcessBench benchmark. The conflict is only apparent: different model classes and different evaluation setups, plausibly both true, so type4 rather than type1.
rationale_B: The hypotheses are compatible because Hypothesis A makes a general claim about standard LLMs, while Hypothesis B focuses on a specific class of advanced reasoning-focused models (o1 and QwQ) that may possess different capabilities.

hypothesis_a: Pre-trained language models can serve as effective inductive reasoners, capable of inducing general rules from given examples.
hypothesis_b: A comprehensive evaluation shows that even advanced LLMs struggle with simple inductive reasoning tasks when tested in symbolic settings.
rationale_A: A makes a general claim that pretrained LMs are effective inductive reasoners; B's finding is explicitly scoped to 'symbolic settings' in a comprehensive evaluation. The qualifier signals a context-dependent evaluation condition rather than a flat opposite claim about the same setting, so type4 rather than type1.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A presents a general claim about LLM capability, whereas Hypothesis B specifies a particular context (symbolic settings) where they struggle, meaning both can be true simultaneously.

topic: NMT vs human robustness to noise
hypothesis_a: Neural machine translation systems are heavily degraded by synthetic and natural noise such as misspellings, in contrast to more traditional translation approaches.
hypothesis_b: Human readers incur a measurable processing cost when reading words with jumbled or scrambled letters, showing that human word recognition is also disrupted by misspelled input, though evidently less catastrophically than neural MT systems.
rationale_A: B explicitly subordinates its claim to A's ('less catastrophically than neural MT systems'), so the two are complementary rather than opposed: both agree NMT degrades more than humans do under noisy/jumbled input. No type1-4 conflict exists here.
rationale_B: Both hypotheses agree that NMT systems are vulnerable to noise; the second hypothesis merely adds a comparison to human processing without contradicting the first.

hypothesis_a: Code-switching/word-borrowing detection can be handled by tagging an entire word with a single coarse-grained 'mixed' label, without further internal distinction.
hypothesis_b: The 'mixed' code-switching label should be expanded to identify the specific languages present at the morpheme level within a single word (intra-word code-switching), rather than a single whole-word tag.
rationale_A: A holds that a single coarse whole-word 'mixed' label suffices for code-switching detection; B holds that this label should instead be expanded to morpheme-level, intra-word distinctions. These are directly opposed prescriptions for the same annotation task (granularity of code-switch labeling), so type1 rather than type4.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that code-switching can be handled using a single coarse-grained 'mixed' label for entire words, whereas Hypothesis B explicitly rejects the use of a single whole-word tag in favor of morpheme-level language identification.

hypothesis_a: Larger and more diverse study populations can be reached through volunteer-based, uncompensated online experimentation platforms such as LabintheWild, which recruit individual participants directly for behavioral studies.
hypothesis_b: Wikibench offers a community-driven alternative to individual-based data curation for AI evaluation, capturing community consensus rather than aggregating individual volunteer responses.
rationale_A: A and B describe two different data-collection paradigms (individual volunteer experimentation vs. community-consensus curation) serving different goals; neither claim negates the other's validity or effectiveness. This is not a contradiction of any type.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses describe different approaches to data collection—one focusing on individual-based recruitment via platforms like LabintheWild and the other on community-driven consensus via Wikibench—and do not present conflicting claims.

hypothesis_a: EchoPrompt improves LLM performance by prompting the model to first rephrase the query before answering it, yielding substantial gains across zero-shot and few-shot prompting, including chain-of-thought settings.
hypothesis_b: Zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting significantly increases the likelihood of harmful and biased outputs when applied to harmful-question and stereotype benchmarks, revealing a safety cost of CoT not captured by accuracy-focused evaluation.
rationale_A: A reports accuracy/performance gains from EchoPrompt rephrasing across zero-shot/few-shot/CoT settings; B reports a safety cost (increased harmful/biased output) specifically for zero-shot CoT measured on harm/bias benchmarks. These concern different evaluation dimensions (task accuracy vs. safety) that can both hold simultaneously, so type4 rather than type1.
rationale_B: The hypotheses address different metrics; one focuses on performance gains in task accuracy, while the other focuses on the trade-off regarding safety and bias.

hypothesis_a: Large language models cannot self-correct their own reasoning through intrinsic self-reflection alone; genuine improvement requires external feedback.
hypothesis_b: LLMs' self-estimated confidence can be leveraged to improve intrinsic self-correction/self-refinement capability, complicating the claim that self-correction is not achievable without external feedback.
rationale_A: A asserts LLMs cannot self-correct via intrinsic self-reflection alone and require external feedback; B asserts self-estimated confidence can improve intrinsic self-correction, explicitly framed as complicating/negating A's no-intrinsic-correction claim. Same question (is unaided intrinsic self-correction possible) with opposite answers, so type1.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that intrinsic self-reflection alone is insufficient for self-correction, whereas Hypothesis B claims that intrinsic methods like confidence estimation can be used to improve self-correction capabilities.

hypothesis_a: The Houlsby adapter architecture inserts an adapter module both after the multi-headed attention sublayer and after the feed-forward sublayer in each transformer layer, i.e. two adapters per layer.
hypothesis_b: The Bapna and Firat adapter simplifies this design by introducing only one adapter module per transformer layer, keeping only the 'top' adapter after multi-headed attention and dropping the 'bottom' adapter after the feed-forward sublayer.
rationale_A: A and B are compatible factual descriptions of two distinct adapter architectures (Houlsby's two-adapters-per-layer vs. Bapna-Firat's single top adapter); B is presented as a simplification of A's design, not a competing claim about the same architecture. No contradiction of any type.
rationale_B: The hypotheses describe two distinct architectural designs; one describes the Houlsby adapter and the other describes a separate, simplified version by Bapna and Firat.

hypothesis_a: The Houlsby adapter approach re-trains the transformer's existing layer normalization parameters separately for every new domain.
hypothesis_b: The Bapna and Firat adapter instead leaves the original layer normalization parameters frozen and introduces new, separate layer normalization parameters for every task, mimicking the structure of the transformer's feed-forward layer.
rationale_A: Houlsby and Bapna-Firat are different named adapter architectures whose layer-norm handling differs by design, not a shared claim about how adapters must work; neither statement asserts the other's approach is wrong, so this is a compatible architectural variant (type4), not a type1 negation.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses describe different adapter architectures (Houlsby vs. Bapna and Firat) and their respective, distinct approaches to layer normalization, meaning they are not in conflict.

hypothesis_a: Misinformation should be defined narrowly, as demonstrably false and inflammatory content.
hypothesis_b: Misinformation should be defined more expansively to also include true information that is misleading and causes harm, a category sometimes termed 'malinformation,' rather than only outright false content.

rationale_B: Hypothesis A proposes the use of explicit projection matrices for vocabulary alignment, whereas Hypothesis B explicitly rejects this approach in favor of an indirect method using relative representations.

hypothesis_b: A comprehensive review that aggregates findings from existing studies can characterize ChatGPT's background, applications, key challenges, bias, ethics, and limitations, offering a generalized perspective without collecting new primary data.

topic: effect of output format constraints on LLM performance
hypothesis_a: Imposing rigid output format restrictions on large language models (e.g., forcing structured formats) reduces their task performance compared to allowing free-form generation.
hypothesis_b: Structuring large language model outputs does not necessarily harm, and can actually improve, task performance; claims that format restrictions hurt performance rest on flawed evaluation.
rationale_A: Both hypotheses make a causal claim about the same variables (output format restriction and LLM task performance) but assert opposite directions of effect -- A says restriction reduces performance, B says it does not harm and can improve performance, explicitly disputing A's causal claim as resting on flawed evaluation -- this direction-of-effect dispute is type3, not a generic type1 negation of a non-causal claim.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that output format restrictions reduce performance, whereas Hypothesis B directly negates this by stating such restrictions do not necessarily harm performance and may even improve it.

topic: code generation vs. tool orchestration for visual reasoning
hypothesis_a: Complex visual reasoning tasks can be solved by having a system generate an explicit program (executable code) that composes vision and language modules, without additional training.
hypothesis_b: Visual reasoning and image editing/generation tasks can be accomplished by having a language model orchestrate external visual foundation models directly, without the system itself generating code.
rationale_A: A explicitly has the system generate executable code, while B explicitly accomplishes the task "without the system itself generating code," a direct negation of the same design point (code generation vs. none) for the same task family (visual reasoning) -- this explicit architectural rejection is type1, not a compatible type4 variation, since the topic itself frames code-generation as the pivotal question both papers answer oppositely.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses propose different, non-mutually exclusive methodologies (code generation versus direct model orchestration) for solving visual reasoning tasks; the success of one method does not preclude the existence or validity of the other.

topic: evaluation paradigms for continual learning in LMs
hypothesis_a: Continual learning ability of language models should be evaluated primarily by domain-specific adaptability and incremental-learning performance across a sequence of new training domains.
hypothesis_b: Continual learning ability of language models should instead be evaluated with a dedicated benchmark that measures whether a model retains time-invariant knowledge, updates outdated information, and acquires new knowledge over time.
rationale_A: Both are prescriptive claims about how continual learning ability in LMs should be evaluated, and B explicitly says its knowledge-retention benchmark should be used "instead" of A's domain-adaptability paradigm as the primary evaluation approach -- a direct methodological negation (type1), not a contextual difference, since both claim to be the correct primary standard rather than complementary facets tied to different architectures/datasets.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that the primary evaluation metric for continual learning should be domain-specific adaptability, whereas Hypothesis B explicitly proposes an alternative paradigm (temporal knowledge updates) instead of the one proposed in Hypothesis A.

topic: role of LLMs in skill-extraction pipelines
hypothesis_a: Skill extraction and standardization from job-posting text can be delivered as a live API service that queries a large language model at inference/request time.
hypothesis_b: For skill extraction, a large language model is better used only during the training stage (to produce training signal for a smaller extraction model), keeping the LLM out of the inference path to reduce latency and improve reproducibility.
rationale_A: A has the LLM queried live at inference time via an API, while B explicitly argues the LLM is "better used only during the training stage ... keeping the LLM out of the inference path," directly negating A's inference-time deployment choice for the same task (skill extraction) -- a genuine design negation (type1), not an architecture-contingent compatible difference (type4).
rationale_B: Hypothesis A proposes using an LLM at inference/request time for skill extraction, while Hypothesis B explicitly states that the LLM should be kept out of the inference path.

topic: scale vs. quality of instruction-tuning data
hypothesis_a: Instruction-following large language models can be effectively built by fine-tuning on a large, automatically constructed instruction dataset.
hypothesis_b: Strong instruction-following and alignment can be achieved with only a small number of carefully selected, high-quality examples rather than large-scale automatically constructed data -- 'less is more' for alignment.
rationale_A: A claims effective instruction-following comes from fine-tuning on a large automatically-constructed dataset, while B explicitly claims strong results come from a small curated set "rather than large-scale automatically constructed data," framing itself as a counter-thesis ("less is more") to A's scale-based approach -- this direct rejection of the necessity of scale is type1, not a compatible dataset-size variation (type4).
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that large-scale, automatically constructed datasets are effective for instruction tuning, whereas Hypothesis B explicitly contradicts this by stating that small, high-quality datasets are more effective than large-scale data.

hypothesis_a: Neural code generation can be improved by using compiler feedback to identify erroneous code and guide correction.
hypothesis_b: CodeRL improves code generation by empirically defining fixed reward values for different unit-test execution outcomes, used as a reinforcement learning training signal.
rationale_A: A proposes using compiler error feedback to correct code, B proposes fixed unit-test-outcome reward values for RL training; these are two distinct, non-competing signal sources for improving code generation and neither claim negates the other, so not a contradiction rather than type4.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses describe different, non-conflicting methods for providing feedback to code generation models: one focuses on compiler error signals and the other on unit-test execution outcomes as reinforcement learning rewards.

topic: Correctness vs relevancy in dialogue evaluation
hypothesis_a: Correctness and relevancy of a dialogue system's response should be evaluated jointly, having users rate 'how relevant/correct is the answer retrieved' as a single combined judgment.
hypothesis_b: Accuracy and relevancy are separate constructs when evaluating dialogue responses: a response can be accurate even if it is not relevant to the question asked.
rationale_A: A claims correctness and relevancy should be judged jointly as a single combined rating, while B claims they are separate constructs that can diverge (accurate but irrelevant); this is a direct yes/no clash on whether the two dimensions are one judgment or two, not a dataset/context artifact, so type1.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A proposes that correctness and relevancy should be treated as a single, combined metric, while Hypothesis B asserts that they are separate, independent constructs.

hypothesis_a: Scaling laws for neural language models were derived under training on unique data for only one epoch, describing a smooth relationship between model/data size and loss.
hypothesis_b: When a small fraction of training data is repeated across epochs, model performance diverges from Kaplan's scaling law, with repeated data becoming harmful to performance for models larger than about 100M parameters.
rationale_A: A's scaling law was explicitly derived under one-epoch unique-data training, and B's divergence is explicitly conditioned on repeated data for models >100M params; the apparent conflict stems purely from a differing training-data condition (unique vs repeated), making the two compatible rather than a real type1-3 conflict.
rationale_B: The hypotheses are compatible because the divergence described in hypothesis B is explicitly attributed to a change in training conditions (data repetition) relative to the scope defined in hypothesis A (unique data).

topic: Granularity of knowledge editing in LLMs
hypothesis_a: Privacy-sensitive knowledge stored in pretrained language models can be located and removed by identifying individual 'privacy neurons' via a cumulative probability-based detection strategy (DEPN).
hypothesis_b: Rather than locating and editing an individual weight, factual knowledge in GPT-like models can be updated by modifying an entire feed-forward network (FFN) layer (ROME).
rationale_A: A targets locating and deleting individual privacy neurons for a knowledge-removal task, while B targets updating factual knowledge via a whole FFN layer for a knowledge-insertion/update task; they address different objectives (privacy deletion vs factual editing) with different granularity, so neither claim contradicts the other.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses describe different approaches and granularities for knowledge editing (neuron-level for privacy vs. layer-level for factual updates) and do not logically negate one another.

hypothesis_a: Instruction-following training data can be generated by producing model responses to human-provided instructions (Self-Instruct).
hypothesis_b: Instead of generating responses to given instructions, instruction-tuning data can be created by generating instructions for existing human-written text found online -- the reverse strategy (instruction backtranslation).
rationale_A: A generates responses given instructions (Self-Instruct) and B generates instructions given existing text (backtranslation); these are two alternative, non-exclusive data-construction directions for the same downstream goal, not opposing empirical claims, so not_contradiction rather than type4.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses describe different, non-mutually exclusive strategies for generating instruction-tuning data: one focuses on generating responses from instructions, while the other focuses on generating instructions from existing text.

topic: Syntactic vs lexical-semantic drivers of brain-LM alignment
hypothesis_a: In studies of brain alignment with language models, syntactic processing tasks are the primary driver of the alignment between brain activity and language model representations.
hypothesis_b: Lexical-semantic content, not syntactic structure, is the main contributor to the similarity between artificial neural network representations and brain (fMRI) responses in the language network.
rationale_A: A claims syntactic processing is the primary driver of brain-LM alignment, and B explicitly states lexical-semantic content -- not syntactic structure -- is the main contributor under the same brain-alignment paradigm; B directly negates A's attribution of the same phenomenon, so type1 rather than a causal-direction (type3) conflict.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A claims that syntactic processing is the primary driver of brain-LM alignment, whereas Hypothesis B explicitly states that lexical-semantic content is the main contributor and specifically excludes syntactic structure from being the primary factor.

topic: Classifier-guided vs classifier-free diffusion for text generation
hypothesis_a: Controllable text generation with diffusion language models can be achieved through classifier-guided diffusion, i.e. using an external classifier to steer the diffusion process toward desired attributes (Diffusion-LM).
hypothesis_b: Sequence-to-sequence text generation with diffusion models can be achieved without an external classifier, using a classifier-free diffusion approach directed by spatial points instead (DiffuSeq).
rationale_A: A addresses attribute-controllable generation via classifier-guided diffusion (Diffusion-LM) and B addresses sequence-to-sequence generation via classifier-free, point-directed diffusion (DiffuSeq); they target different generation tasks with different design choices, not competing claims about the same setting.
rationale_B: The two hypotheses describe different, non-exclusive methodologies (classifier-guided vs. classifier-free) for achieving text generation with diffusion models.

topic: Joint vs separate representation-space clustering for multimodal self-supervised learning
hypothesis_a: Effective self-supervised multimodal representation learning from audio, video, and text can be achieved by clustering on a joint multimodal representation space, combined with a pairwise contrastive loss across modalities (MCN).
hypothesis_b: Effective self-supervised representation learning from audio and video can be achieved by clustering on separate, modality-specific representation spaces via cross-modal deep clustering (XDC), rather than a single joint representation space.
rationale_A: A claims effective multimodal self-supervised learning requires a joint multimodal representation space, while B explicitly claims separate modality-specific spaces work better 'rather than a single joint representation space' -- a direct same-setting negation, not a dataset/architecture-driven type4 difference.
rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that effective learning can be achieved via a joint multimodal representation space, whereas Hypothesis B directly contradicts this by proposing separate modality-specific spaces instead of a joint one.

topic: Whether correct input-label mapping matters for in-context learning
hypothesis_a: The correctness of input-label mapping in few-shot demonstrations matters little to in-context learning performance; models can perform comparably well even with random or incorrect labels.
hypothesis_b: Ground-truth (correct) input-label mapping in in-context learning demonstrations does matter and significantly influences in-context learning performance.

hypothesis_a: Text generation can be steered effectively by exemplar-based adaptive decoding that directly incorporates retrieved exemplars into the decoding process, without requiring a separate re-ranking step over retrieved candidates.
hypothesis_b: Effective retrieval-augmented text generation requires an explicit intermediate re-ranking stage between retrieval and generation, as in retrieve-rerank-rewrite pipelines that rerank retrieved templates before rewriting them into output.
rationale_A: A claims effective decoding can incorporate retrieved exemplars without a separate re-ranking step, while B claims effective retrieval-augmented generation requires an explicit re-ranking stage; these are directly opposed necessity claims about the same pipeline component, not merely a contextual/architecture artifact.

hypothesis_a: Semi-supervised sequence learning using RNNs and autoencoders (e.g., pretraining a sequence autoencoder or RNN language model before task training) is an effective way to improve text classification and other sequence models.
hypothesis_b: Effective transfer learning for text classification with LSTM-based language models requires novel fine-tuning techniques (discriminative fine-tuning, slanted triangular learning rates, and gradual unfreezing) rather than relying on RNN/autoencoder pretraining alone.

hypothesis_a: Using linguistically motivated subword segmentation units, rather than purely statistical ones, can affect neural machine translation quality for the Tamil-English language pair, though results are mixed.

topic: Syntactic parsing in semantic query graph generation
hypothesis_a: Semantic parsing for question answering over knowledge bases can be performed by using a syntactic parser (e.g. a CCG or dependency-tree parser) to help construct the semantic query graph from the input question (Reddy et al., 2014, large-scale semantic parsing without question-answer pairs).

hypothesis_b: Mixed-language (Hindi-English) automatic speech recognition can instead be achieved by reusing existing monolingual acoustic models together with a phone-mapped lexicon and a modified language model, rather than training a new bilingual acoustic model (Bhuvanagiri & Kopparapu, 2010, an approach to mixed language ASR).

hypothesis_a: Adversarial techniques can be used to evaluate dialogue generation systems, by training a discriminator to distinguish machine-generated responses from human-written ones as a proxy for response quality (Kannan & Vinyals, 2017, adversarial evaluation of dialogue models).

rationale_B: The hypotheses are complementary; hypothesis B explicitly acknowledges the use of adversarial techniques for evaluation (as stated in A) and proposes their use as an additional method for training.

rationale_B: Hypothesis A asserts that learning a linear mapping requires a large seed lexicon of thousands of pairs, whereas Hypothesis B contradicts this by stating the task can be achieved with as few as 25 pairs.

topic: Understandability evaluation of controlled natural languages
hypothesis_a: Attempto Controlled English (ACE) has been empirically shown to be easier and faster for people to understand than a conventional ontology notation, when used for authoring or reading OWL statements (Kuhn, 2013, the understandability of OWL statements in controlled English).

topic: nature of language: symbol system vs. use
